title: Medbot - service overview
description: Read TOP-DOWN. Section 1 answers 'is the product meeting its promises', section 2 'is it refusing what it must', section 3 'where does the time go', section 4 'are the parts underneath healthy'. Every panel has an (i) description saying what good looks like and what a bad reading MEANS - a dashboard you cannot read without asking its author is not observability.

panels.title: 1 - Is the product meeting its promises? (Phase 1 NFRs)
TTFT p50  (NFR <= 0.8s)
panels.description:
Time to FIRST streamed token, median. The perceived-latency SLI: it is how fast the app FEELS, not how long the answer takes.

STREAMING ONLY - non-streaming requests have no first token, so curl tests leave this empty. Empty means 'nobody streamed', not 'fast'.

Bad reading: embed and rerank both run on CPU BEFORE generation starts, so both sit inside TTFT. MEASURED over 20 warm in-corpus questions: embed 152ms, retrieve 18ms, rerank 1270ms, generate-to-first-token 463ms, giving TTFT p50 1.90s / p95 2.65s.

An earlier version of this note said embed ~1.6s and 'TTFT cannot go below ~4s'. That was a COLD reading - the first embed after boot loads the model - taken before SGLang was given room to capture prefill CUDA graphs. The floor with a free reranker is 152+18+463 = 633ms, which is UNDER the 0.8s NFR: the target is reachable. It needs rerank cut from 1270ms to ~167ms, which means moving it off CPU. Fewer candidates and ONNX do not get there - ONNX measured only 8% faster, with identical top-4 ordering.

panels.title: TTFT p95  (NFR <= 2.0s)
panels.description:
Slowest 5% of first-token times. p50 tells you the typical experience; p95 tells you the one people complain about.

A p95 far above p50 means a queue or a cold path, not uniform slowness.

panels.title: Request p95  (<= 6s)
panels.description:
Full end-to-end time, all outcomes mixed.

Cache hits are included and record THEIR OWN duration, not the generation they avoided - that was a real bug (I8.2): replaying the original 11s on every hit made the cache look like a regression, and p95 got worse the more traffic it served.

panels.title: Cost / request p95  (<= $0.001)
panels.description:
Spend for the 95th-percentile request.

$0.000000 is the CORRECT reading when self-hosted: local venues price at $0 by construction. Anything above zero means a hosted leg served - either you chose it, or your local engine failed over without you noticing.

Zero is always observed now, never skipped: absent and zero are different answers on a spend dashboard (I5.4).

panels.title: Requests / sec
panels.description: Answered queries per second, every outcome. The denominator for every rate on this dashboard - read the panels below as fractions OF this.

panels.title: 5xx error rate
panels.description:
Server errors as a fraction of answers.

A refusal is NOT an error and must never appear here: declining to give a dosage is the product working. Only 5xx counts.

panels.title: local-sglang - TTFT p50
panels.description: Time to first token for THIS venue. A local GPU and a hosted API differ by an order of magnitude; the combined panel above averages whichever venues happened to serve. — CUMULATIVE since the API last restarted, deliberately NOT rate()[5m] like row 1. rate() of a flat counter is 0, and histogram_quantile over all-zero buckets is NaN, so a rate-based panel reads NaN whenever no request landed inside the window — which on a bursty dev box is most of the time. Cumulative trades recency for always meaning something, and makes an empty panel mean exactly one thing: this leg has not served since the restart. Row 1 keeps rate() because it answers 'how are we doing NOW'; this row answers 'which leg is slow', which does not need to be recent to be true.

panels.title: 2 - SAFETY: is the product refusing what it must? (D18)
Refusals by category
panels.description:
WHICH safety rule fired: emergency, self_harm, dosage, diagnosis, injection, prescription, medication_change, harmful.

WHY BY CATEGORY: `answers_total{kind="refused"}` cannot tell an emergency from a dosage question, so a guardrail that quietly STOPPED matching looks exactly like one nobody triggered. That is precisely how the self-harm rule shipped broken (I7.1) - every gerund phrasing ('thinking about hurting myself') fell through into retrieval and returned 'I don't have reliable information', and no counter moved.

Watch for a category going to zero and STAYING there.

panels.title: Answers by kind
panels.description:
The product's shape: grounded / no_answer / refused / degraded.

All grounded  -> guardrails are not firing; test a dosage question.
All no_answer -> retrieval is broken, or the index is empty.
Any degraded  -> the kill switch or the daily spend cap is active.

panels.title: Declines by path - and which one costs money
panels.description:
Two different gates produce the same word to the user:

retrieval_gate    nothing scored above no_answer_threshold; the model was NEVER called. Free. ('What is the capital of France?')
model_abstained   retrieval cleared the coarse gate, the model read a FULL prompt (~1,000 tokens) and said it had nothing. ('Side effects of semaglutide?' - the corpus has diabetes text that scores plausibly.)

Rising model_abstained is a real bill for saying 'I don't know'. If it dominates, raise no_answer_threshold so the free gate catches more.

panels.title: Silent quality degradation
panels.description:
Times the pipeline served a WORSE answer instead of failing.

Today that means the reranker timed out and fusion order was served instead - the user cannot see it and the response says nothing.

This must sit near ZERO. It was invisible until now: RERANK_TIMEOUT was 2.0s against a measured rerank p95 of 2.425s, so the fallback fired on well over 5% of queries while every dashboard stayed green (I6.5/I6.6). A timeout below the p95 of what it guards makes the degraded path the NORMAL path.

panels.title: 3 - Where does the time actually go?
Stage latency p95
panels.description:
Per-stage p95: condense, embed, retrieve, rerank, generate.

EXPECTED SHAPE: rerank dominates, then generate. embed and retrieve should be small.

embed climbing  -> ml-service is CPU-starved or being called per-request instead of batched.
retrieve climbing -> Qdrant is optimising after an ingest, or the index outgrew RAM.
condense present -> a follow-up was rewritten; it only runs for anaphoric or very short questions, so it should be rare and small.

This panel is where you look when Jaeger says a request was slow and you want to know whether it is slow for everyone.

panels.title: End-to-end latency p95 by outcome
panels.description:
Same latency, split by what the request produced.

refused should be the FASTEST line by far - guardrails fire before retrieval and before the model. If refusals cost as much as grounded answers, the guardrail is running too late to save you money or liability.

panels.title: Cache hit rate
panels.description:
Fraction of requests served without generating.

Only GROUNDED answers are cached (D10) - refusals and no_answers deliberately are not, so a heavy safety-testing session drags this down and that is correct.

Flat zero on repeated identical questions means the cache KEY is changing when it should not. The key includes prompt version, corpus version, index version, collection and a digest of every model that could serve, so changing any of those invalidates on purpose.

panels.title: Cache events/sec
panels.description:
The raw hit/miss counts behind the ratio, per layer.

Useful when the ratio looks wrong: it separates 'few hits' from 'no traffic at all'.

panels.title: Tokens/sec by venue and direction
panels.description:
Token throughput, labelled by WHICH venue produced them.

The venue label is what separates self-hosted from paid: tokens on local-vllm or local-sglang are free, tokens on groq or openai are an invoice.

If local goes to zero while groq climbs, your engine died and failover is quietly paying for it - which is exactly what happened while SGLang was down.

panels.title: 4 - Are the parts underneath still healthy?
Serving venue circuit breakers
panels.description:
0 = closed (healthy) - 1 = half-open (probing) - 2 = OPEN (skipped).

An OPEN leg is being bypassed entirely, so requests silently move down the chain. Find out WHY before dismissing it: a self-hosted leg opening means you are now paying a hosted one.

EVERY leg is republished on every transition, not just the one that moved - a gauge written only when a venue is touched leaves the others reporting stale values forever (I5.4).

panels.title: Infra dependency circuit breakers
panels.description:
Redis and Postgres breakers. 0 closed, 2 OPEN.

Neither is required to answer (D21): losing Redis costs the cache, losing Postgres costs history. The breakers make an outage CHEAP (~0ms instead of a timeout per call) - which also removes the latency symptom you would otherwise notice, so this panel is the only signal that anything is wrong.

panels.title: Rate limiting by scope
panels.description:
429s by which limit tripped (per-session, per-IP, global).

Should be flat zero during manual testing. Sustained rate limiting on a real deployment means either abuse or a limit set below normal traffic.

panels.title: Errors by type
panels.description:
Typed domain errors, not raw exceptions.

degradable=true  the system had a fallback and used it (cache bypass, history off).
degradable=false the request genuinely failed.

retrieval-unavailable is the one to watch: embedding is the FIRST step, so without a vector there is nothing to search and the request is fatal rather than degraded.

panels.title: Answer volume by kind (cumulative)
panels.description:
Raw counters rather than rates - the totals since this process started.

Useful for a manual test session, where 5-minute rates round to nothing but you still want to confirm each of the four outcomes actually happened at least once.

Note these RESET on restart. Prometheus keeps the old series, which is why a long-dead container can still show errors that no longer exist anywhere (I6.4).
